tier_reason: performance_summary.md and README carry the wrk table (Zig 80,700, C++ 40,715, C 32,976 req/s) from public code (blade_core.{c,cpp,zig}, bench.sh, Makefile), but the measurement is not valid as a comparison: blade_core.zig never calls read() and closes with the request unread, while blade_core.c/.cpp read first, and the Zig row carries 701k write errors; under the no-valid-measurement precedent (dp::thread_pool, fc_malloc) this goes to D. No CPU, kernel or compiler versions are stated either, so it could not be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s on loopback (first-party, single run): Zig 80,700 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.98x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (2.45x, derived from page data); the same table marks the Zig row '701k write errors (buffer overrun)' and the C/C++ rows 0 errors. Not a like-for-like measurement (the Zig server skips the request read).
corrections.caveats: Not a valid language comparison. blade_core.zig accepts, writes the fixed response and closes without ever reading the request, whereas blade_core.c and blade_core.cpp read() once before writing; closing a socket with unread data makes the kernel reset the connection, which fits the 701k write errors the page reports for Zig (the page blames a 'buffer overrun'), so the Zig row measures less work and an abortive close rather than codegen. The Makefile builds Zig with a bare 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per the source banner) and Rust with plain rustc (no -O), against gcc -O2 / g++ -O2 for C and C++; none is -O3. Each server is a single-threaded blocking accept loop that closes every connection, while wrk keeps HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and must reconnect after every response, so throughput is dominated by connection setup and teardown. Ports differ (8080, 8081, 8083) and only the Zig server sets SO_REUSEADDR. CPU, kernel, compiler and wrk versions are not stated; single run. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise. The README itself recommends 'Zig (if tuned)'. One commit, 0 stars.
corrections.why_faster: Not a language effect: the Zig server skips the read() syscall and closes with the request unread (abortive reset, 701k write errors on the page), and its binary is an unoptimised Debug build, so nothing on the page shows Zig codegen beating C or C++.

notes: Downgrade C to D: the faster side does less work (no read of the request) and aborts connections, the Zig build is Debug against -O2 C/C++, and no hardware is stated; keep as a flagged entry with these shortcomings (an orchestrator could also treat it as invalid evidence of the 'faster side skips the work' kind, but the keep-and-document precedents for timed-but-incomplete work went to D). Repo is MIT, 0 stars, one commit dated 2025-07-12 (stale).

tier_reason: The README Benchmarks section shows fib 194,671 vs workflow (C++) 150,407 echo TPS, TLS 1.3 echo 103,427 vs uSockets 103,972, all from the author's own lesismal/go-*-benchmark repos (public code; workflow built -O3 Release in frameworks/workflow/build.sh) as single runs on GitHub-hosted 4-vCPU runners with no CPU model stated, so first-party C. The HttpArena rows are from a third-party harness (128 stars) whose fib entry is maintained by lesismal, with no CPU model stated; they show fib behind nginx at baseline-4096, so they do not lift the tier.

corrections.claimed_speedup: HTTP/1.1 echo (first-party go-http1-benchmark, single GitHub Actions run, 10,000 connections, 1 KiB): fib 194,671 TPS vs Sogou workflow (C++) 150,407 (1.29x, derived from page data), memory 32 MB vs 14 MB; workflow has no pipeline result (it does not support pipelining). TLS 1.3 echo 103,427 vs uSockets + BoringSSL (C) 103,972 (a tie, fib 0.5% behind) and TLS 1.3 pipeline 690,000 vs 735,000 (fib 0.94x, derived). WebSocket echo: fib's 138,592 is the top row, but the runners-up shown (uws_events 129,363, fnet 126,401) are Go servers, and the C++ uWebSockets server's row is not in the README table. The README itself claims parity ('level with or close to') with the C, C++ and Rust servers, not a win. HttpArena (third-party harness): baseline-4096 3,164,504 vs nginx 3,284,513 (0.96x); baseline-h2c-256 12,891,491 vs nginx 2,456,329 (5.2x, derived from page data) but behind agensio (C++) 15,185,367.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27; HttpArena entry built with CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' (frameworks/fib/Dockerfile). Baselines: workflow v1.1.0 built from source with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and its server main.cc with c++ -std=c++11 -O3 -DNDEBUG (go-http1-benchmark frameworks/workflow/build.sh); uSockets server.c with cc -std=c11 -O3 -DNDEBUG on pinned uSockets and BoringSSL (go-tls-benchmark frameworks/usockets/build.sh); nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module at -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (HttpArena frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile). Compiler versions not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party single runs on noisy shared GitHub runners (the README says read differences of a few percent as ties); 2 vCPUs for the server, where workflow keeps its default 20 handler threads plus pollers. It loses to axum on HTTP/1 echo (236,244 vs 194,671), to uSockets on TLS pipelining (690,000 vs 735,000) and to the Go servers uws_std, fnet and uws_events on WebSocket pipelining; the workflow pipeline row is missing because workflow does not support pipelining. 'uws_events'/'uws_std' are Go servers on UIO, not uWebSockets; the C++ uWebSockets entry of go-websocket-benchmark is not shown in fib's table. In HttpArena (fib entry maintained by lesismal, CPU model not stated) it is slightly behind nginx at baseline-4096 (3,164,504 vs 3,284,513) and far ahead of nginx on h2c (12,891,491 at 256 connections vs 2,456,329), but agensio (C++) beats it on h2c (15,185,367) and h2 (14,744,015 vs 5,634,126 at 256), libreactorng (C) beats it on pipelined-4096 (43,424,448 vs 20,397,414) and mongoose (C) on most WebSocket profiles; fib leads static-tls-1024 (1,229,892 vs agensio 1,191,970 and nginx 720,869). No LICENSE file in the repo.

notes: Numbers match the README; tier C stays (author-run benchmark repos, single runs, no CPU model). Main shortcoming: the only clear win over a C/C++ server is HTTP/1 echo vs workflow (1.29x); TLS is a tie, the WebSocket runner-up the record cited (uws_events) is a Go server, and in HttpArena nginx is ahead at baseline while agensio (C++) is ahead on h2/h2c. No license (reference); 27 stars, last commit 2026-10-11.

tier_reason: HttpArena results JSON (site/data/results/ioxide.json and sibling nginx/h2o/mongoose/agensio/libreactorng/libioma files) carries every number in the record, with public entry code (frameworks/ioxide, frameworks/nginx with -O3 -march=native) and stated build settings, but the suite and ioxide share an owner (MDA2AV) and the README gives only '64-core dedicated hardware' with no CPU model, so first-party C, not A.

corrections.caveats: The ioxide repo is owned by the same GitHub account as the HttpArena suite (MDA2AV), so tier is C rather than B even though every entry runs through one public harness. The ioxide Dockerfile notes that moving from .NET 11 preview.6 to preview.7 took baseline-4096 from 4.11M to 3.90M with no change to the entry; the saved 4,111,381 is the preview.6 figure, and at the 3.90M the currently pinned preview.7 gives, the lead shrinks to about 1.19x nginx, 1.07x h2o, 1.05x mongoose and 1.10x agensio (derived from page data). It is behind libreactorng (4,377,377) and libioma (4,255,834), both C io_uring servers, at baseline-4096, so the win over nginx comes from io_uring against nginx's epoll rather than from C#; behind nginx at limited-conn-4096 (2,543,314 vs 2,626,297); and on baseline-h2-1024 the 3.7x over nginx is against nginx's slow h2 path, while h2o (15,633,023) and agensio (C++, 14,210,433) both beat ioxide's 12,235,767, and agensio also leads static-h2-1024 (1,420,432 vs 950,009). The h2 path uses pure-C# ioxide.http2 with OpenSSL encrypting in userspace; h1 TLS uses OpenSSL handshake plus kernel kTLS; h3 rides the bundled C libraries ngtcp2 and nghttp3. The repo README gives no throughput numbers against C servers. Results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; entries are minimal hand-written handlers (nginx is a custom C handler module, ngx_http_httparena_module.c), and the baseline-4096 profile mixes GET and POST with query parsing, not static files. CPU model not stated, so not tier A. The .NET build uses Server GC and the runtime-async preview feature; README marks ioxide experimental.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7 / runtime 11.0.0-preview.7, dotnet publish -c Release with ServerGarbageCollection and runtime-async=on (HttpArena frameworks/ioxide/Dockerfile and ioxide-arena.csproj, ioxide NuGet 0.7.211); nginx 1.31.4 configured with --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' on debian:trixie (frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile); h2o built with clang, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and -march=native.

notes: All record numbers match the HttpArena JSON files (baseline-4096 4,111,381 vs nginx 3,284,513, h2o 3,641,609, mongoose 3,707,598, agensio 3,558,559; pipelined 53,376,982 vs nginx 4,037,345 and libreactorng 43,424,448; h2 12,235,767 vs nginx 3,320,285). Tier C stays: same owner as the suite, no CPU model; C io_uring servers (libreactorng, libioma) beat it, and h2o and agensio beat it on h2, so the win is io_uring against epoll rather than the language. MIT, 56 stars, last commit 2026-10-10.
